strings.name: Dilma Rousseff
strings.role: President of the New Development Bank; former president of Brazil
strings.summary: Dilma Rousseff became Brazil’s first woman president in 2011 and was removed by the Senate through impeachment in 2016. Previously minister of mines and energy and presidential chief of staff, she has led the New Development Bank since 2023, working on multilateral cooperation in infrastructure and sustainable-development finance.
strings.coverageNote: Checked through 18 November 2026, including the recorded Hongqiao Forum address on 6 November and the COP31 exchange reported on the 12th. NDB elections, effective terms and later public events are distinguished. Institutional financing goals are not completed project outcomes.
strings.influence.rationale: Brazil’s first woman president, whose administration and impeachment shaped national politics, later became involved in multilateral affairs through the New Development Bank.
strings.facts.f1.label: Economics education
strings.facts.f1.value: Graduated in economics from the Federal University of Rio Grande do Sul in 1977. Later attended master’s and doctoral programmes at Unicamp but did not complete the theses and defences required for those degrees.
strings.facts.f2.label: Early political experience
strings.facts.f2.value: Opposed Brazil’s military government as a young activist, was arrested in 1970 and tortured while imprisoned, and was released in late 1972. She then moved to Porto Alegre, resumed her studies and turned to open political activity.
strings.highlights.h1.title: Energy policy and infrastructure coordination
strings.highlights.h1.text: In Lula’s government, worked on electricity policy and the Luz para Todos programme, later coordinating the Growth Acceleration Programme, PAC. Government agencies, companies and local institutions implemented these programmes jointly; their development goals are not personally achieved economic results.
strings.highlights.h2.title: Impeachment outcome and political dispute
strings.highlights.h2.text: The Senate removed her over supplementary budget decrees without legislative approval and delayed agricultural-subsidy transfers but did not approve the additional public-office disqualification. She denied an impeachable offence and called the process a coup. The outcome and her position are distinguished; this was not a criminal corruption conviction.
strings.timeline.t1.title: COP31 exchange reported
strings.timeline.t1.text: Instituto E+ reported that she received research materials during COP31 in Antalya and stressed advancing a just energy transition together with technology. The 12th is the report date; the precise time of the exchange was not verified and the accompanying video was not watched.
strings.timeline.t2.title: New NDB term begins
strings.timeline.t2.text: The Board of Governors unanimously re-elected her on 19 March for a term running from 7 July 2025 to 6 July 2030. Election and term-start dates differ; 2030 is the scheduled endpoint, not a record of service already completed.
strings.timeline.t3.title: Elected NDB president with immediate effect
strings.timeline.t3.text: The Board of Governors unanimously elected her, explicitly effective that day. Lula’s visit to the Shanghai headquarters on 13 April was a later public event and does not move her term’s start to April.
strings.timeline.t4.title: Senate removes her from the presidency
strings.timeline.t4.text: The Senate approved removal by 61 votes to 20. A separate vote fell short of the requirement to bar her from public office, preserving her political rights. These were two distinct decisions.
strings.timeline.t5.title: Participates in multilateral creation of the NDB
strings.timeline.t5.text: During her Brazilian presidency, the five BRICS founding countries signed the bank’s agreement in Fortaleza. It entered into force on 3 July 2015; signature in 2014 and the following year’s launch are different stages.
strings.timeline.t6.title: Becomes Brazil’s first woman president
strings.timeline.t6.text: Took office after winning the 2010 election and began a second term in 2015. Her first election, two inaugurations and the termination of her mandate in 2016 are recorded separately.
strings.timeline.t7.title: Becomes presidential chief of staff
strings.timeline.t7.text: Succeeded José Dirceu as the first woman to head the Casa Civil, coordinating government policy and advancing PAC. This was a cabinet office serving the president, not a prime ministership.
strings.timeline.t8.title: Becomes minister of mines and energy
strings.timeline.t8.text: Took responsibility for national energy affairs in Lula’s government, building on earlier state-level administrative experience. She also chaired Petrobras’s board; that role should not be confused with the company’s CEO.
